insights.title: No detectable association between ARG and faecal risk
insights.finding: Pathogen and faecal risk move together (rho = +0.72). ARG risk shows no detectable association with faecal risk (rho = -0.03). The composite top quarter leaves out 18 of the 24 highest-ARG sites.

examples: O12 (Oslo): ARG 0.68, faecal 0.32, composite 0.37
T12 (Toulouse): ARG 0.65, faecal 0.09, composite 0.26
T10 (Toulouse): ARG 0.64, faecal 0.02, composite 0.23
T13 (Toulouse): ARG 0.60, faecal 0.30, composite 0.34
O11 (Oslo): ARG 0.60, faecal 0.33, composite 0.37

insights.limitation: A null result on n=96 cannot rule out a small link (|rho| below about 0.22). One sample per site, and the scaled ARG index is defined upstream by OneAquaHealth.
insights.next_step: Rank and triage sites on ARG as its own dimension, and re-sample the high-ARG / low-faecal sites to confirm.

challenge.detail: Bootstrap (1000 resamples): faecal-vs-ARG rho = -0.03, 95% CI -0.22 to +0.17 — the interval spans zero. With the city effect removed it is +0.00. Contrast: pathogen-vs-faecal rho = +0.72 (95% CI +0.60 to +0.82), positive in 5/5 cities (lowest +0.49). Caveat found by the same check: inside cities ARG is weakly related to pathogen risk (rho = +0.22, p=0.033), so the supported claim is 'no detectable association with faecal risk', not 'independent of everything'.

insights.title: Cities differ on each risk dimension — the composite score hides it
insights.finding: On the composite score the five cities are not clearly different (p=0.060). Split by component, pathogen, faecal and ARG risk each differ between cities, and not in the same direction: Coimbra is highest for pathogen, Oslo for ARG.

examples: pathogen: highest in Coimbra (0.32), lowest in Ghent (0.10); adjusted p<0.001
faecal: highest in Benevento (0.43), lowest in Ghent (0.25); adjusted p=0.029
ARG: highest in Oslo (0.44), lowest in Coimbra (0.29); adjusted p=0.029

insights.limitation: Each city was sampled in a single campaign (May, June-July or September), so city and season cannot be separated in this snapshot.
insights.next_step: Compare cities component by component, and sample all cities in the same season.

challenge.detail: Three component tests, Holm-corrected: pathogen p<0.001; faecal p=0.029; ARG p=0.029. Composite alone: p=0.060. Differences hold after correction.

insights.title: Two observed risk profiles emerge
insights.finding: The 96 sites fall into 2 groups: 31 sites with elevated pathogen + faecal · average ARG; 65 sites with low pathogen + faecal · average ARG. ARG risk is nearly the same in every group, so the groups differ in their level of pathogen and faecal contamination, not in ARG.
insights.limitation: Clusters describe observed risk composition only; they do not explain why a site has that profile, and k is chosen by silhouette, not theory.
insights.next_step: Profile each group against land use and season with repeated sampling.

challenge.detail: Compared with 200 simulated datasets that keep the same correlations but have no clusters (and get the same choice of k): real silhouette 0.380 vs simulated mean 0.331 (95th percentile 0.367); p=0.015. The grouping is stronger than correlation alone would produce.

insights.title: At some sites the composite score hides one very high component
insights.finding: 6 sites have one risk component at least 0.35 above their composite score — the average masks a substantially elevated dimension.

examples: T17 (Toulouse): composite 0.53 but faecal 1.00
T5 (Toulouse): composite 0.43 but faecal 0.85
T10 (Toulouse): composite 0.23 but ARG 0.64
T12 (Toulouse): composite 0.26 but ARG 0.65
O14 (Oslo): composite 0.25 but ARG 0.60

insights.limitation: Follows from how the composite is defined (mean of three components); descriptive.
insights.next_step: Report and triage by the highest component, not by the composite alone.

challenge.detail: Arithmetic on the observed components, not a modelled claim — nothing to shuffle away.

insights.title: A few sites stand well above their own city's norm
insights.finding: 9 sites sit at least 1.5 standard deviations above their city's mean composite risk — local hotspots worth first inspection.

examples: C5 (Coimbra): +2.6 SD above its city mean (composite 0.78)
BN2 (Benevento): +2.6 SD above its city mean (composite 0.73)
G9 (Ghent): +2.4 SD above its city mean (composite 0.36)
O17 (Oslo): +1.9 SD above its city mean (composite 0.42)
BN10 (Benevento): +1.9 SD above its city mean (composite 0.62)

insights.limitation: Based on one sample per site; an outlier may reflect that day, not a trend.
insights.next_step: Re-sample flagged sites and their upstream and downstream neighbours.

challenge.detail: Descriptive ranking of observed values inside each city; it makes no cross-city or predictive claim.

insights.title: Across these five cities, landscape features do not predict risk in an unseen city
insights.finding: Trained on four cities and tested on the fifth, the model beats a 'predict the average' baseline for 0 of 4 targets. So landscape context is used here to explain and to generate hypotheses, never to forecast.

examples: pathogen: error 0.160 vs baseline 0.148; rank agreement inside a held-out city +0.13 on average
faecal: error 0.157 vs baseline 0.153; rank agreement inside a held-out city +0.03 on average (computable in 4 of 5 cities; elsewhere the model predicts a constant)
ARG: error 0.129 vs baseline 0.128; rank agreement inside a held-out city -0.05 on average (computable in 1 of 5 cities; elsewhere the model predicts a constant)
composite: error 0.107 vs baseline 0.103; rank agreement inside a held-out city +0.20 on average

insights.limitation: 96 sites and five cities is a small test; a larger network or repeated sampling could reveal signal this snapshot cannot.
insights.next_step: Do not rank unsampled sites by modelled risk; send samplers instead.

challenge.detail: Each city is held out in turn, so the model never sees the city it is scored on. The baseline is the mean of the four training cities. Elastic-net and shallow gradient boosting were both tried; neither beats the baseline.

insights.title: 42% of citizen site registrations need fixing before use
insights.finding: 30 of 71 citizen-registered sites are flagged: 10 test or placeholder names, 3 with latitude and longitude swapped, and 19 entries that are really 5 places registered several times. Separately, 39 registrations lie more than 50 km from any lab-monitored site; that is noted, not treated as an error.
insights.limitation: Rules catch what they are written for. A swap is only detected when the corrected point lands near a known site; a real site with a generic name can be flagged as a placeholder.
insights.next_step: Run the same checks in the app at the moment of entry: confirm swapped coordinates and offer 'add a visit to the existing site' instead of a new one.

challenge.detail: Deterministic rules on the actual submissions; every flag names the rule that raised it and can be re-run.

insights.title: Candidate signal: vegetation fragmentation within 250 m
insights.finding: Across 96 sites, vegetation fragmentation within 250 m shows a positive rank association with composite risk (Spearman rho = +0.28, p=0.006 before any correction).
insights.limitation: Cross-sectional, one sample per site; association is not causation and the effect is small.
insights.next_step: Treat as a hypothesis: write it down now and test it on new samples or a new city before acting on it.

challenge.detail: Challenge 1 — city confounding: inside cities rho = +0.18 (p=0.078) vs +0.28 overall; same sign in 5/5 cities. Passed. Challenge 2 — multiple testing: this is one of the strongest of 59 features screened. Shuffling risk between sites of the same city 500 times, the best of 59 reaches |rho| >= 0.32 by chance in 5% of shuffles; family-wise p = 0.90. Not distinguishable from the best chance finding — kept as a hypothesis only.

insights.next_step: Treat as a hypothesis: write it down now and test it on new samples or a new city before acting on it.

insights.title: High-risk sites that the landscape candidates do not explain
insights.finding: 3 sites are in the top third for risk yet sit far from wastewater stations with unfragmented vegetation. Whatever drives their risk is not in the landscape data.

examples: BN4 (Benevento): composite 0.38, 6.7 km from a wastewater station
BN15 (Benevento): composite 0.37, 11.7 km from a wastewater station
T6 (Toulouse): composite 0.36, 5.4 km from a wastewater station

insights.limitation: Built on two candidate patterns that are themselves only exploratory, and on one sample per site; the mismatch could be noise or an unmapped source.
insights.next_step: Put these first in line for repeat sampling and an upstream source search.

challenge.detail: The sites are real and their values are observed, but the list is defined by patterns that did not clear the multiple-testing correction — so it is a place to look, not a finding.

insights.title: Distance to crop fields does not hold up as a risk signal
insights.finding: Across 96 sites, distance to crop fields shows a negative rank association with composite risk (Spearman rho = -0.22, p=0.029 before any correction).
insights.limitation: Cross-sectional, one sample per site; association is not causation and the effect is small.
insights.next_step: No action — keep it out of site prioritisation.

challenge.detail: Challenge 1 — city confounding: inside cities rho = -0.06 (p=0.535) vs -0.22 overall; same sign in 3/5 cities. The association mostly reflects differences BETWEEN cities, not between sites — rejected.
